items.title: Earl Turbinton Interview, 1990-09-01
items.q: But in meeting with Jules Kahn, he took me to this building

ctx.x: milieu of what was happening there. Well, the period that the Jazz Workshop developed and... Well, the time that... I mean... Sorry, go ahead. Sorry. The period that we developed the Jazz Workshop was one that was born out of frustration for myself and many of the young jazz musicians during that period of time. And that there were no schools in this immediate area or schools that we knew about to learn more about the techniques of improvisation as far as chord scale relationship. It was pretty much trial and…

And prior to that, people like Nat Paralot and Alvin Batiste, Harold Batiste, the American jazz quintet that was Ellis Marsalis and Alvin Batiste and other persons, Chuck Beatty at one time, I think Otis DuVernay. And even earlier than that, I heard people like Ed Blackwell when I was very, very young. But there was no format for younger players to come and learn from those type players. We were searching to develop, if you will, a school of sorts so that a young developing player might get my experience, Alvin…

but more like a temple or a place to come and bathe yourself in music and to pray in music. And when we did play in that room, not only were the musicians very telepathic, but many, many times, and as a listener, if you were there, I'm sure you may have experienced the same thing, where sometimes we would be transported to a zone where it felt like the whole room was of one mind and the music was happening right there. Because a great majority of what we played was happening on the spot, even though it might have…
